q-75832.name: Question 1
q-75832.problem:
The following table gives the values of functions $g(x)$ and ${g}^{′}(x)$ at some points. Find $({g}^{-1})^{′}(7).$

| **$x$** | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-6$ | $9$ | $-1$ |
| $4$ | $7$ | $-4$ |
q-75832.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({g}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=7,$ we have

$$
({g}^{-1})^{′}(7)=\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(7))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${g}^{-1}(7)=4$ and ${g}^{′}(4)=-4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}({g}^{-1})^{′}(7) & =\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(7))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{g}^{′}(4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-76112.name: Question 2
q-76112.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1).$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0).$
q-76112.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ (x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,0.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $x=-2$ since the logarithm is not defined for negative numbers. Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{2(x+2)}{2x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 0+1)+\frac{2(0+2)}{2\cdot 0+1} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =0+4 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110341.name: Question 3
q-110341.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+5x+2.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
q-110341.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ {x}^{3}+5x+2 & =2 \\ x({x}^{2}+5) & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3}+5x+2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\cdot 0+5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-342582.name: Question 5
q-342582.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2{e}^{2x} \\ {f}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =2{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {f}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ {f}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =2\cdot 4 \\ {f}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =8.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(4,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
